1:
When the love began is pressed first. Gill offers several ways of reading it: that Israel was a child, rebellious and disobedient, and yet loved; or that though a child, weak and foolish, he was loved; or that in the infancy of his civil and church state the Lord loved him with a special love, choosing that people above all others and giving them his law and his worship, which he gave to no other nation. Henry says God had done more for them than for any people under heaven: when they first multiplied into a nation he set his love on them and chose them because he loved them; when they were weak and helpless, foolish and froward, outcasts and children exposed, then God loved them and bore them as a nurse bears the sucking child, nourishing them and suffering their manners.

Calvin puts the love earlier still. What was their condition when they were emancipated in Egypt? They seemed like a man half dead, with no vigour remaining; and the Lord stretched out his hand to a people in that hopeless state, drew them as it were from the grave, and restored them from death to life. The nativity of this people, Calvin says, was their coming out of Egypt: the covenant with Abraham had been made four hundred years before, and the patriarchs were counted his children, but God wished his Church to be as it were extinguished when he redeemed it, so Scripture speaks of the liberation as of a birth. And the love came before the birth: I not only loved him when a child, he has God say, but before he was born, for the liberation was the nativity and my love preceded it, Egypt being a grave without a spark of life.

Whether the second clause looks forward divides them. Wesley takes the adoption first: God adopted him for a son and as a son brought him out of servitude, but Israel the first adopted son was a type of Christ the firstborn, and the history of the coming out a type of the coming out of Christ. Henry says the words have a double aspect, speaking historically of the calling of Israel and prophetically of the bringing of Christ from the same country, the former being a type and pledge of the latter. Ellicott will not allow it in this context: there cannot be a prophecy of the Christ here, since obstinate conduct and rebellion would then be involved in the prediction. He grants that the New Testament quotes the passage to illustrate that the true Son of God was also submitted in his youth to the hard schooling of a cruel exile, and says the calling of the Messiah out of Egypt gave a new indication of the cyclical character of Hebrew history. Clarke calls the whole chapter a very pathetic representation of the tender regard of God for Israel, by metaphors chiefly borrowed from the conduct of mothers toward their offspring.

The calling of the next verse is a different one. Calvin marks the change: God effectually called the people out of Egypt, but here calls by the outward voice of teaching through his prophets, who are not named but plainly meant. The indefinite form makes the indignity more evident, since they had been called so often and by so many and had still refused; the people were called not once or twice but constantly, and God sent not one messenger but many prophets one after another, all without benefit. Gill says the more the prophets called, the further they went; Ellicott glosses the pronouns, that as they, the prophets, called, so they, Israel, went from them, seeking to avoid the voice and presence of the men of God; Wesley names Moses and Aaron among those who urged the whole house of Israel, and dates the apostasy from the desert.
3:
The picture is of a child learning to walk. Clarke calls it an allusion to a nurse teaching a child to walk, directing how it lifts and lays its feet and supporting it by the arms, and calls the passage truly pathetic. Wesley says God helped as a nurse does, bearing them up, and that they would not acknowledge him in it. Gill adds that God went before them himself in the pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night. Ellicott would render it, yet it was I who guided the steps of Ephraim.

The first word Calvin says occurs nowhere else in Scripture, and he canvasses what it is. One lexicon makes it a verb meaning to teach to go; another a noun meaning a footing, so that the line runs, as for me, my footing was for Ephraim, that is, I attended him on foot as a nurse does a child. Calvin sides with those who make it a noun, since the other way requires a change of letter at the beginning of a word, which grammarians do not allow. The sense either way is that as a child is by degrees accustomed to walk, the nurse having regard to his infancy, so God led Israel as far as his feet could bear.

Why the kindness is recited Calvin states. God amplifies the sin by showing that no kindness, over however long a time, could allure or reform them. It was enough that a people brought from the grave to the light of life should have repudiated every instruction; but he adds that he never ceased to show his love and gained nothing by it, the depravity of the people being incurable. Ellicott turns the clause about not knowing on his own age: the refusal to own a divine origin for ideas which bless and beautify life, treating them instead as the voice of nature or the development of humanity, he calls one of the commonest sins.

The cords of the next verse are set against other cords. Gill notes that Ephraim had been compared to a heifer in the previous chapter and is here drawn, but not with such cords as cattle are, rather with such as men are; so God drew Israel through the wilderness by bestowing favours and making promises. Ellicott sets them against the cords by which unmanageable beasts are held in check, so that Israel is led with bands of love and not compulsion, and would render the last clause, and gently towards them gave I food to eat. Calvin makes it an argument: God had not dealt with them as slaves or oxen are dealt with, but by the cords of a man, which means humane government, so the people could not complain of rigour, as though he had used a hard wedge for a hard knot. Had he done so, they might have pleaded that it was no wonder they disobeyed; but since such kindness had no influence, their wickedness must be counted irreclaimable.

The lifting of the yoke Clarke explains from the field. There is an allusion, he says, to moving the yoke forward on beasts hard at work, to let the cool air in between it and the neck and prevent the heat which with the sweat would scald them; he has often done it himself at the land ends in ploughing, and the laying of meat is the bite of grass given to encourage them on afresh. God, he adds, mingled privileges and comforts with his precepts to make the people at once righteous and happy. Wesley says the same of a husbandman who in due season takes the yoke from his labouring oxen and removes the muzzle that kept them from eating at work; and Calvin has God say that he never laded them as oxen are laden, but raised the yoke upon their cheeks.
5:
Whether Egypt is open to them divides the readings. Gill offers three senses: that they should not go there again to be captives, but into a harder bondage in Assyria; that they should not go for shelter; or that they should not go to seek help as they had done, since there would be no need of it did they but return to the Lord. Clarke reads it as a settled purpose: God brought them out that the nation should never go back, but since they have forfeited his favour they shall go to Assyria instead, because they refused to return to him; which view, he says, removes every difficulty. Ellicott takes both clauses as questions instead, shall he not return into the land of Egypt, and shall not the Assyrian be his king, and glosses the last word as returning to God. Wesley notes that the Assyrian would rule them with rigour and cruelty, and that the reason of it all was their obstinacy in idolatry.

Calvin makes the verse a closed door. The people had hoped that if the Assyrians proved too strong there would still be a refuge in Egypt among friends with whom they had a treaty, and the prophet exposes the vain confidence: the way they counted on is shut. The reason turns on the same word twice, for they thought there would be a free passage into Egypt and yet had been unwilling to pass over to God when he so often called; a return into Egypt is therefore denied to men who would not return to him. When men perversely resist God, Calvin adds, they hope in vain for free movement in any direction, since the Lord holds them bound, as wild beasts too ferocious are shut in cages, and frantic men bound with strong bands.

The sword that follows is set against their defences. Gill takes it for the sword of the Assyrians, resting on all their cities, not the chief only. Calvin explains why the verse is needed: it was hard to persuade a proud people that the overthrow was at hand while they saw themselves furnished with defences, so the prophet adds that their fortified cities would not keep the enemy out, and that there is no reason to trust fortresses which the Lord can destroy by the sword. He notes that the verb means to abide, to encamp, and sometimes to fall upon, and prefers the last, though he allows the rendering that the sword shall be upon the cities until it consume them.

Clarke supplies the history. Israel was agitated by wars foreign and civil, king after king slain by the man who took his place, whole tribes carried captive, and at last the capital taken after a three years siege; so the sword rested on their cities until all was ruined.

What the branches are is the last. Calvin says the Hebrews often use the word for bars or bolts and oftener for branches, so that some take it for towns and villages, which are the branches of a city, while others make it sons, growing from their parents as branches from a tree, which he thinks far-fetched. He does not disapprove the first, but prefers his own reading of bolts as more suitable, the word standing as a part for the whole, since bolts were one part of the fortifications. Ellicott calls the English rendering incorrect and would translate, then shall the sword be brandished amid his cities and destroy his princes, the word for princes being literally bars, since the defenders of a state are aptly called its bulwarks. Wesley keeps to the towns and villages, and takes the counsels for those the people followed against all the prophets gave them; Keil and Delitzsch add that they deserved to be utterly destroyed for it, and would have been, had not the compassion of God prevented.
7:
Whether the people are bent or in suspense is the whole question of the verse. Gill takes the first: there is a propensity in them through prevailing corruption, the bias of their minds is that way, they are bent upon it and pertinaciously abide in it, and will not be reclaimed by any means or methods, though they had professed themselves the people of God. But he reports another rendering, my people are in suspense, like a man who hangs in the air and neither ascends nor descends; on that reading they are in doubt what should be done to them or what they should do, either about a return of God to them or about their own return to him, inclining rather not to return.

Calvin sets out the same alternatives at more length. Some explain the word as perplexed, so that the prophet says the people suffer a just punishment in being anxious and looking about them and finding no comfort: it is no wonder they are tormented with great anxiety and find no end to their evils, since men who rebel against the Lord deserve to be bound fast by him, and it is the fruit of their defection that they are now so full of sorrow and of despair. Others make it a complaint against men who deliberated whether they ought to repent, taking suspense for doubt: they debate the matter as doubtful when they are exhorted to repent, and cannot decide, inclining now to one thing and now to another, as though the subject itself made deliberation necessary; whereas what is right is in no way hid from them, but being unwilling they seek excuses for doubting by evasions, while the prophets cry and no one extols God.

Calvin decides the question from the noun that follows. Some render it turning away, taking the affix passively of their own alienation from God, and others render it conversion; but the Hebrew doctors hold that the word is always used in a bad sense and never means anything but rebellion or apostasy. Since that is so, Calvin inclines to turning away, and concludes that the second exposition, which makes the people deliberate whether to hear the prophets, cannot stand.

The second clause is read three ways. Wesley takes the callers for the prophets and says scarce any one would hearken and obey. Ellicott observes that the verse drops the imagery of the chapter altogether, using neither the unfaithful wife nor the recalcitrant heifer nor the baker piling his furnace, but homely literal commonplace: the people were called by sufficient means to the highest worship, and were bent on the lowest. Clarke abandons the common rendering for another, that though they call on him together because of the yoke he will not raise it, and he shall receive no refreshment, which ties the clause back to the figure of the yoke a few verses earlier.
8:
Every voice reads the verse as a debate carried on within God himself, and every one of them warns at once that the debate is a figure. Henry calls it a gracious debate concerning Israel’s case, a debate between justice and mercy in which victory plainly inclines to mercy’s side; not that there are any such struggles in God as there are in us, or that he is ever fluctuating or unresolved, for he is in one mind and knows it, but these are expressions after the manner of men. He sets out the two pleadings as speeches. Justice proposes that Ephraim be given up as an incorrigible son is given up to be disinherited, as an incurable patient is given over by his physician, delivered into the enemy’s hand as a lamb to the lion to be torn in pieces, made as Admah and set as Zeboim, and Henry grants that Ephraim deserves it and that God would do them no wrong. Mercy answers as a tender father reasoning with himself how he can find in his heart to cast off an untoward son: they have been a people near to God, there are yet some good among them, theirs are the children of the covenant, if they be ruined the enemy will triumph, it may be they will yet repent.

Wesley states the figure in a sentence, that God is never fluctuating or unresolved, and that the words show what severity Israel had deserved and yet how divine grace would be glorified in sparing them. Clarke puts it as a standing contest, justice demanding the punishment and mercy pleading for the life, and takes the weariness in the words seriously: the heart is oppressed and weary with repenting, with so frequently changing its purpose. All this, he says, though spoken after the manner of men, shows how merciful and how loath to punish the God of heaven is, and he asks what sinner or saint upon earth has not been a subject of these gracious operations.

Calvin presses the figure hardest, because he sees a use made of it he will not allow. God assumes the character of one deliberating so that none may think he hastily fell into anger, or that being soon excited by excessive fury he devoted to ruin those who had lightly sinned. That is the whole force of it: God does not deliberate as to himself, but with reference to men, accommodating himself to our ignorance and putting on a character foreign to himself as far as a regard for our salvation will bear. Calvin refuses the inference that God is therefore changeable, or that his purpose waits quietly upon what men will do and can determine nothing except through their free will; he answers that the one and simple will of God does not exclude such accommodation. The threat inside the deliberation he takes at full weight, that the Israelites were little short of the lot of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the relenting he explains by the same father who on seeing his son’s wicked disposition suddenly feels a strong displeasure and then, being seized with relenting, is inclined to spare him.

Ellicott hears the passage as one of the most pathetic in Hebrew prophecy, the bow of promise gleaming on the darkest cloud; as the prophet loved his faithless bride, so Jehovah continued to love his people, and the repeated how expresses the most extreme reluctance. He identifies Admah and Zeboim as cities of the plain destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah and often named as the type of irremediable catastrophe. On the last clause he departs from the common rendering: not turned within me but turned against me, a violent revulsion of feeling, divine compassion pleading with divine justice.
9:
The verse answers the debate of the one before it, and the voices differ chiefly over what exactly is being refused. Wesley reads the not returning against the practice of war: conquerors that plunder the conquered city carry away the wealth of it, and after some time return to burn it, and God will not do so. Calvin reads it as a limit set on a punishment already begun. Because the kingdom of Israel had in part been laid waste already, the promise is that the second overthrow, which he would presently bring, would not be such as would consume the whole; though he shall again gird himself to punish the sins of the people, he will restrain himself so that the vengeance shall not proceed to the destruction of the whole people. Gill takes the same measure inwardly: the people are deserving of wrath as others, being by nature children of wrath as the rest, and though the Lord often chastises and afflicts them, it is not in wrath, or however but in a little wrath as it seems to them, since all was poured upon his Son their surety.

On the reason given, that he is God and not man, Calvin holds hardest to the figure he had already insisted on. God is exempt from every passion, and what is called the fury of his wrath is the relation between his nature and our sins; Scripture says God is angry because we imagine him so according to the perception of the flesh. He then makes the clause a remedy for a particular fault, that we rely with difficulty on the promises of God because we imagine him to be like ourselves, and he tells the trembling conscience to take instant hold of this declaration as a shield against every kind of diffidence. He also narrows the address: the prophet speaks not promiscuously to all the Israelites but to the faithful, the remnant among a corrupt people, since this saying was never meant to relieve the sorrow of hypocrites. Clarke states the same ground more briefly, that mercy triumphs over judgment because God cannot be affected by human caprices and will not punish former offences as a man would; judgment, he says, is his strange work. Ellicott admires the passage as one drawing its illustrations from human emotions and yet repudiating all human weakness, so that justice and mercy, both alike infinite, adjust themselves beyond the power of human experience and imagination, and he finds that blending in the title of the Holy One in the midst of thee. Wesley makes the same title covenantal, a holy God and in covenant, though not with all yet with many among you.

The last clause divides them. Wesley and Clarke take it of destruction and reach for the same comparison, Wesley that God will not enter to destroy as he did Sodom, Clarke that the holy place is in Ephraim and God is in it, and he will not go into the cities as he did into Sodom and Gomorrah. Ellicott reports that reading as the one the ancient versions carry, entering as a destroyer, but prefers a rendering many commentators take from the Hebrew, in wrath rather than into the city. Calvin canvasses two other explanations and rejects both: that no city but Jerusalem would be entered, which does not suit a prophet speaking of the ten tribes and not of Judah, and that the people would survive but be left without city or kingdom or united body, which he calls forced, a mere refinement which of itself vanishes.
10:
What it is to walk after the Lord is the first question, and Calvin sets himself against the common answer. To expound it of the obedience of the people, as it is done by interpreters, does not seem right to him; it is certain that no people can be restored except they repent, but the prophet here handles another thing, that the Lord will show himself a leader to a people who had been dispersed. As long as they were scattered in Assyria and in other distant lands they were without any head, as a mutilated body; when the ripened time of restoration came, God proclaimed himself the leader of his people, and in this manner the people were gathered to him. Gill goes the other way and takes the walking as discipleship after the Messiah, whom he calls Jehovah our righteousness, that Jehovah whom the Jews pierced and at whose sight they shall mourn, being converted to him; they will follow as sheep go after their shepherd, as subjects follow their prince, as soldiers march after their leader, walking not after the flesh as they now do but after the Spirit. Wesley takes it of the remnant who shall hear and obey.

The roaring is heard as many different sounds. Calvin makes it the terror of God against those who would hinder the return: many will be the enemies and many will labour to set up opposition, but the Lord will fill all with dread and restrain all their efforts, so that neither Assyrians nor Egyptians shall impede the people, since a decree God had determined could not be nullified by the whole world; he notes a similar mode of speaking in Joel. Wesley reports the reading of the Chaldee, that it is the word of the Lord which roars as a lion, and adds that Christ is called the lion of the tribe of Judah, and that the voice of the gospel was heard far, as the roaring of a lion. Clarke gives the roar a date: it is the majestic voice by which Cyrus shall make his decree, and the trembling is a state of commotion, everyone hurrying to avail himself of the opportunity to return to his own land. Ellicott renders the clause as going up after Jehovah, who roars as a lion, illustrates the figure from the lions that accompanied Egyptian monarchs to the battlefield, taking his example from Rameses II in his battle with the Kheta, and glosses the trembling as an awe-stricken joy at the divine summons; the west, he says, means the coast and islands of the Levant.

On the birds the voices largely agree, and divide only on how far the promise reaches. Gill hears in the trembling either the trembling of birds at the roaring of a lion or the trembling motion of their wings in flight, and takes it for swiftness, reporting also a rendering that they shall come with honour, that is with readiness and cheerfulness. Wesley has some hastening out of Egypt whither they fled for shelter and others like doves out of Assyria, and calls the placing a seasonable and comfortable promise. Clarke makes the placing concrete, that they shall have their temple once more and all their holy ordinances. Calvin uses the birds of the enemies rather than the exiles, comparing Egyptians and Assyrians to doves and sparrows for the fear God would strike into them. Ellicott renders the last clause as causing them to dwell, and holds that the prophetic word looks past the restoration of the sixth century to a gathering of some from east and west out of all the places where they are hidden, a broader accomplishment that will more than fulfil the yearnings of the spiritual Israel.
12:
Three of the voices open by saying that the verse is in the wrong place. Gill holds that here properly we should begin a new chapter, as many interpreters and commentators do, since the predictions concerning the call and conversion of the Israelites and their return to their land are finished, and a new discourse begins by comparing the characters of Ephraim and Judah. Clarke agrees that it does not well unite with what goes before, belongs to another subject, and should begin the following chapter, as in the Hebrew. Ellicott says the same, that it should stand as the first verse of the next chapter just as in the Hebrew text, and that what follows is a distinct composition, a new commencement of judgment and incrimination closing with one more utterance of divine promise.

On the compassing about with lies, Calvin presses the military figure in the word. It means that the Israelites acted unfaithfully not in one way or in one thing, but as when a man besieges an enemy with a great army, so that they were full of innumerable frauds with which on every side they surrounded God. This, he says, is what hypocrites are wont to do: they transform themselves in various ways and ever seek some new subterfuge, and when they are caught in one sin they pass into another, so that there is no end to their deceit. His lesson is that men in vain make excuses before God, for in contriving pretences to deceive him they deceive themselves. Gill locates the deceit in worship: the ten tribes surrounded either the prophet, professing great regard for what he said, or rather the Lord himself, whom they pretended to serve when they worshipped the calves at Dan and Bethel, and would have it thought that they did not worship the calves but the Lord in them and by them. Wesley reduces the clause to a sentence: Ephraim means most of the people of Israel, who play the hypocrite with God still.

The second clause divides them sharply. Wesley, Clarke, Gill and Calvin all take it as praise. Wesley reads it that while idolaters are slaves to the devil the true worshippers of God, like princes, rule with him, and that Judah retains purity, or at least truth of worship, and comparatively is faithful, adhering to the holy prophets and priests and other saints. Clarke finds an allusion to the night when Jacob wrestled with the Angel and had his name changed to Israel, one that rules with God; that glory the Israelites lost by their idolatry, but Judah still retained the true worship and alone deserved the name. Calvin makes the sovereignty legitimate because it was joined to a pure and lawful priesthood, both divinely instituted, whereas the other kingdom was spurious from the revolt from the family of David, when a new king changed both the law and the worship and erected new temples; yet he insists the prophet speaks comparatively and does not wholly excuse. On the saints he canvasses the possibilities and declines both the reading that makes the plural word a name for God and the reading that makes it the sanctuary, which he calls strained and without example, preferring the holy fathers or the whole Church, and inclining to include the angels. Ellicott alone turns the clause into an accusation. He reports that the received rendering came from Jewish scholars who saw here a reference to the reign of Hezekiah, objects that it is opposed to the controversy with Judah named a little later, and adopts instead a rendering that Judah still roves unbridled towards God and towards the faithful Holy One, so that the inconstancy of Judah is set against the faithfulness of God. Clarke, faced with a comparable alternative from Newcome, records it and says he does not see what we gain by the change.
